newsitem.title: USA: Clinton lets U.S. firms bid on Chile jet order.
newsitem.headline: Clinton lets U.S. firms bid on Chile jet order.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton has given U.S. aircraft manufacturers permission to submit bids to Chile for the purchase of fighter jets, an administration official said on Thursday.

Although Clinton would have to approve an actual sale of jets to Chile, it marks the first time since the 1960s that Washington has allowed U.S. firms to even enter the competition for high-tech weapon sales to Latin America.
"The president has authorized the firms to share technical data with the Chilian government," the administration official said.

Noting that the White House was conducting a review of arms sales in Latin America, the official said permission was granted to make the bids because Chile had set a March 31 deadline for submitting offers.

"We said, okay, you can go share the marketing information with them," the official said, noting "it wouldn't be fair" to deny the firms the chance to submit bids when arms policy for the region may change.
Chilean defense officials have said they were interested in buying Lockheed F-16 Falcon fighters as part of a plan to modernize the country's aging air fleet.
U.S. manufacturers will have to compete with European aircraft, including Swedish JAS-39 Gripen jets and French-made Mirage 2000-5 planes, El Mercurio newspaper reported in Santiago.
The air force, which wants to buy 16-18 jets, was expected to make a decision by the end of the year.

Clinton's decision to ease the restrictions on sales to Chile was the result of pressure from weapons manufacturers and the recent decision by Peru to buy 18 Russian-built MiG-29 fighter jets, El Mercurio said.
The possible sale of the F-16s was strongly opposed by Argentina, which shares a long border with Chile, it said.

Chile, which returned to civilian rule in 1990 after 17 years under the military, has been gradually replacing vintage weaponry with newer equipment, including a fleet of used Mirage jets purchased from Belgium in 1995.
Chile's interest in the F-16s and its maintenance of one of the region's highest defense spending rates sparked fears that it risked starting a new South American arms race.

The ban on weapons sales to Latin America was imposed back when much of the region was under military rule. The return of democracy to most countries has increased pressure from companies and governments to lift the restrictions.
